simple: Type checking lets you label what kind of value each variable or function input should be, like `number` or `string`. Studio then warns you, before you even play, if you mix them up, like passing text where a number belongs. This catches bugs early and makes autocomplete smarter. Labels are optional, so you can add them a little at a time.
analogy: Type labels are like the shaped holes in a toddler's shape-sorter toy. If the hole says "star" (number), Studio complains when you try to push a square (string) through it, before anything breaks.
keyPoints: Put `--!strict`, `--!nonstrict`, or `--!nocheck` on the first line to pick how strict checking is.
`--!strict` checks everything, `--!nonstrict` only checks what you labeled, and `--!nocheck` turns checking off.
Label a variable with a colon: `local coins: number = 0`. Mistakes show up in the Script Editor and Script Analysis window.
Basic types are `nil`, `boolean`, `number`, and `string`. Roblox classes like `Part` and enums like `Enum.Material` are types too.
Add `?` to allow `nil`: `local target: Player? = nil`.
Label function inputs and outputs: `local function add(x: number, y: number): number`.
Table types use braces: `{number}` is a list of numbers, and `{[string]: number}` is a dictionary from text to numbers.
Make your own types with `type`, combine types with `|` (either one) or `&` (both), and share them from a ModuleScript with `export type`.

terms.type: The kind of value something is, like number, string, or Part.
terms.type annotation: A label after a colon that says a value's type, like `x: number`.
terms.type inference: Luau figuring out a type by itself. `local x = 5` is inferred as a number.
terms.gradual typing: You can add type labels to some code and not others.
terms.strict mode: `--!strict`. Every variable is checked, using labels or inferred types.
terms.type error: A warning that a value is the wrong type, like giving a string to a number parameter.
terms.optional type: A type with `?` that can also be `nil`. `string?` means a string or nil.
terms.literal type: A type that only allows one exact value, like `true` or `"Hello world!"`.
terms.type cast: Using `::` to tell the checker to treat a value as a certain type, like `value :: any`.
terms.any: A type that turns off checking for that value. It can be anything.
terms.union type: Either one type or another, written `number | string`.
terms.intersection type: Must match both types at once, written `A & B`.
terms.generic: A type with a blank to fill in later, like `List<T>`. `List<string>` is a list of strings.
terms.export: Making a type defined in a ModuleScript usable in other scripts.

example.title: A typed damage function
example.code:
--!strict
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

-- Our own type for weapon stats
type Weapon = {
	Name: string,
	Damage: number,
}

local sword: Weapon = { Name = "Sword", Damage = 25 }

-- Inputs and output are labeled
local function dealDamage(humanoid: Humanoid, weapon: Weapon): number
	humanoid:TakeDamage(weapon.Damage)
	return humanoid.Health
end

-- Player? means this can be a Player or nil
local function findPlayer(name: string): Player?
	return Players:FindFirstChild(name) :: Player?
end

local target = findPlayer("Builder")
if target and target.Character then
	local humanoid = target.Character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
	if humanoid then
		print("Health left:", dealDamage(humanoid, sword))
	end
end

-- dealDamage(humanoid, "Sword") would show a type error in Studio
explain: `--!strict` turns on full type checking for this script.
`type Weapon` describes what a weapon table must look like: a string name and a number damage.
`dealDamage` says it needs a `Humanoid` and a `Weapon`, and returns a number.
`findPlayer` returns `Player?`, so Studio reminds you to check for `nil` before using it.
Passing a plain string instead of a Weapon would be underlined as an error before you even press Play.

watchOut: Putting `--!strict` below other code. It must be on the first line.
Forgetting that `Player?` can be `nil`. Check `if target then` before using it.
Using `:: any` everywhere to make warnings go away. That hides real bugs.
Thinking type errors stop the game. They are warnings in the editor; the game still runs, and a wrong type can still crash at runtime.
